Authorities urge Kinshasa residents to remain calm while monitoring contacts and imported cases. Continued vigilance and testing are ongoing. Published date reference: 2026-08-11.

article.articleSummary:

The seventh case, Gede EWP, was not reported initially, as his family considered the wound minor. In June 2026, the Buleleng PKPP vaccinated 430 dogs in Bubunan in response to the bites. The dog was a stray that hid in a warehouse; the boy’s father, who was washing a car there, witnessed the bite. After biting Gede EWP, the dog was killed by the father. No dog sample was collected, and one bite went unvaccinated due to underreporting.

article.articleSummary: Personal hygiene is highlighted as a simple yet crucial measure to reduce the spread of infectious diseases in Vietnam. To interrupt transmission, the article notes three components: source, route, and susceptible hosts, with hands as the main conduit. Regular handwashing with soap under running water for at least 30 seconds removes most pathogens responsible for diarrhea and respiratory infections, and routine cleaning of frequently touched surfaces is advised. It emphasizes preserving natural barriers through oral/nasal hygiene (daily saline rinses) and skin care, plus bathing to prevent secondary infections. Community responsibility is stressed: covering coughs/sneezes, disposing of tissues, and washing hands afterward. Five daily habits include handwashing at key times, not sharing personal items, clean clothing, environmental cleaning, and respiratory hygiene. Dengue, spread by Aedes mosquitoes, requires bite avoidance and vector control, while vaccination against measles, chickenpox, and influenza complements hygiene. Article by Dr. Nguyen Minh Hien, Hanoi.

article.articleHeadline: How drug-resistant TB evades detection in standard tests
article.articleSummary: Rifampicin-resistant TB is not reliably detected by standard tests that screen only the 81-base-pair RRDR of rpoB. Non-RRDR mutations outside RRDR cause resistance, enabling ineffective treatment and ongoing transmission. A review by IIT-Guwahati and IIT-Madras cites non-RRDR mutations in North-East India, Eswatini, Myanmar, Peru, and South Africa; in Eswatini, about 30% of drug-resistant TB cases carried such mutations missed by routine tests. Resistance can arise from changes to rifampicin binding or from co-occurring mutations that boost bacterial fitness. Moving beyond RRDR, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) detect broader resistance; Deeplex Myc-TB has identified V170F and I491F mutations in sputum and stool. In rural labs, MAS-PCR and HRMA offer faster, cheaper alternatives, while nanopore sequencing promises portable, real-time detection. For high-burden countries like India, adopting non-RRDR diagnostics is essential to halt silent spread.

article.articleHeadline: Yellow Fever spreading by mosquitoes in Africa, thousands die every year! There could be a risk in India.
article.articleSummary: Yellow Fever, a viral disease transmitted by Aedes, Haemagogus, and Sabethes mosquitoes, primarily in Africa and parts of the Americas, causes 67,000–173,000 severe infections and 31,000–82,000 deaths annually, per WHO. Transmission occurs in three cycles: sylvatic (jungle) via primates, intermediate, and urban when infected humans enter vector-rich areas. Incubation is 3–6 days; early symptoms include fever, headache, myalgia, weakness, nausea. About 15% progress to severe disease with jaundice, dark urine, bleeding, organ failure, and shock; fatality in severe cases reaches about 50% within 7–10 days. India is not endemic, but vaccination and passenger certificates are required for travelers from yellow fever–affected countries; the certificate becomes valid 10 days after vaccination and, under current WHO rules, remains valid for life. There is no specific antiviral treatment; vaccine provides long-term protection.

article.articleHeadline: What Is African Swine Fever? Disease Detected Among Pigs at Kunnamkulam Farm in Kerala
article.articleSummary: African swine fever (ASF) detected among pigs at the Pig Breeding Unit of Kerala's Animal Husbandry Department in Kunnamkulam on Aug 10, 2026. Samples tested at the National Institute for High Security Animal Diseases laboratory in Bhopal confirmed infection. ASF is highly contagious among pigs and does not infect humans. The district declared a 1-km infected zone and a 10-km surveillance zone around the farm, with movement controls on pigs and pork distribution under the Centre's Plan of Action; restrictions began Aug 9. A Rapid Response Team is coordinating disease-control measures. Strict biosecurity guidelines urge farmers to avoid introducing new pigs for at least three weeks, isolate newcomers, restrict visitors and vehicles, and disinfect footwear, vehicles and equipment. Swill feeding should be avoided or boiled for 20 minutes if unavoidable; avoid feeding slaughterhouse waste. Farmers should prevent contact with wild boars and report abnormal pig deaths immediately.

triage.headline_ja: アフリカ豚熱とは？ケララ州クンナムクラムの養豚場で豚に検出
triage.triage_reason: アフリカ豚熱（ASF）は豚のみに感染し人には感染しない動物疾病で、発生農場周辺で移動制限・監視区域が設定され地域当局により管理されているため、公衆衛生上の懸念は低い。
triage.notes: ASFは豚間で高い伝染性を持つが人には感染しない。ケララ州で感染ゾーン・監視ゾーンが設定され、迅速対応チームが対応中。人の健康リスクはなく、動物衛生上の問題として地域管理下にある。

article.articleHeadline: Health screenings for foreign workers: The aim is to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
article.articleSummary: Croatia’s Ministry of Health, by late July, mandated that third-country nationals entering Croatia on visa regimes and renewing temporary residence must undergo a health examination for acute and chronic infectious diseases and receive vaccinations as needed based on vaccination status. Applicable to residents from visa-requiring countries such as India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Egypt, the process requires Form 18a to assess health and vaccination status. A key condition for granting temporary residence is proof of no active tuberculosis and not being a carrier of typhoid (Salmonella Typhi) or paratyphoid (Salmonella Paratyphi). If not fully immunized against diseases in Croatia’s compulsory vaccination program, revaccination is performed. Individuals with TB or carrier status are ineligible. For renewals, the health examination must be issued by the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) and relevant county public health institutes, with Form 18a submitted by a registered home-country health facility.

article.articleHeadline: Panic Over Dirty Water Supply in Dhamtari's Bania Para Ward; Eighteen People Contract Jaundice and Typhoid.
article.articleSummary: Jaundice and Typhoid outbreak in Bania Para Ward, Dhamtari city, Chhattisgarh, linked to contaminated drinking water from a defective pipeline. More than 15 residents affected, with several hospitalized and two in critical condition. Water reportedly foul and insect-infested; residents had raised concerns for days, but officials initially did not act. After media attention, Nagar Nigam’s Water Chairperson Akhilesh Sonker visited, ordered laboratory testing of water samples, and initiated pipeline repairs. Citizens are advised not to consume tap water, and many are buying bottled water. Water samples have been sent to a laboratory; results are awaited. Affected individuals include Ahmed Raza and numerous others from Bania Para Ward; locals demand a high-level investigation and accountability for negligent officials amid an ongoing outbreak.

triage.headline_ja: ダムタリのバニア・パラ地区で汚染水供給によるパニック発生、18人が黄疸と腸チフスに感染

article.articleHeadline: Three migrant workers test positive for malaria in Anavilasam; preventive measures intensified
article.articleSummary: Three migrant workers tested positive for malaria in the Anavilasam area of Idukki district, a cardamom plantation region near Kumily. Infections were detected during targeted screening of migrant laborers; patients received medication and follow-up care. Health authorities conducted contact smears, mass blood smears, and Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) in the affected area. A panchayat meeting chaired by Rejimoal Shiby outlined intensified preventive measures, including mandatory blood testing for all workers employed by plantation owners, establishments, labor contractors, and accommodation providers in the panchayat. Incoming workers from other states will be screened for malaria and filariasis within three days of arrival and must pass a Primary Health Centre check-up with a fitness certificate proving malaria-free status before starting work. Establishments must submit worker details to Ward Health and Sanitation Committees; legal action under Public Health Act, 2023 may be taken against those enabling disease spread.

article.articleHeadline: In Balaghat, the Baiga belt is hit by malaria and diarrhea; 7 children dead, 45 children admitted to hospital.
article.articleSummary: Malaria, diarrhea, typhoid, pneumonia, and skin infections are affecting children in Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh, India, particularly in Baiga belt villages of Korka, Bondari, Kundeksa, and Adori in the Birsa area during the monsoon. In the last ~1.5 months, 7 children (ages about 4–10) have died, while 45 children are admitted at the district hospital, many in serious condition. Health teams have been deployed to screen and treat pediatric patients, and to promote clean water, sanitation, and preventive measures during the rainy season. Medical College Jabalpur and ICMR Jabalpur teams visited to assess health and sanitation issues. Local MLA Anubha Munjare and Civil Surgeon Dr. Nilay Jain announced ongoing surveillance and care to identify cases early and prevent further spread and outbreaks.

article.articleHeadline: Stray dog-bite crisis in UP: Lucknow gives 15k anti-rabies shots a month, Ghaziabad 10k
article.articleSummary: UP grapples with a stray dog-bite crisis as anti-rabies vaccination campaigns show high exposure. Lucknow averages 15,000 post-exposure shots monthly, Ghaziabad about 10,000 (Jan 2024–Sept 2025), with Lucknow sometimes exceeding 20,000 (Feb 2024). Agra, Kanpur Nagar and Varanasi also report high caseloads. Experts warn official counts may underrepresent ground reality due to rural and marginalised populations not accessing post-exposure care. Central data record UP dog-bite totals: 2022 1,91,361; 2023 2,29,921; 2024 1,64,009; Jan 2025 20,478. RTI from Gorakhpur shows Jan–Sept 2024 monthly vaccinations 2,051–3,452, rising to 11,987 (Jan 2025) and 13,085 (Feb 2025); Kanpur Dehat reports 6,463 (Jan 2024) rising to 9,293 (Mar 2025). A Lucknow bench seeks a two-week inter-departmental committee on shelters, sterilisation, vaccination and public awareness. May 19, 2026 Supreme Court judgment upholds Article 21 right to movement and allows stray removal from sensitive zones; Animal Birth Control Rules 2023 do not grant an absolute public-space right.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue count rises to 15 in Gurgaon, Haryana tally 105
article.articleSummary: Dengue in Gurgaon, Haryana: 15 confirmed cases in Gurgaon, taking Haryana’s tally to 105 (66 government, 39 private hospitals). District counts show Jhajjar 24, Karnal 10, Sonipat 8. Most infections are mild with high fever and low platelets; several cases show advanced symptoms, but dengue shock syndrome/ARDS have not been seen. Severe thrombocytopenia requiring platelet transfusion and fluid buildup in pleural/abdominal cavities have occurred. Max Hospital reports more advanced symptoms; about one dengue patient per day in OPD; Manipal notes a modest rise (4-5% vs last year) with one serious case. Labs: 27 dengue testing laboratories; 39,054 samples tested to date, 449 today. Public health measures include 1.5 crore house visits with 17,113 houses having larvae; 267 wards and 1,070 beds reserved; private labs restricted to Rs 600 for NS1/IgM ELISA testing.

article.articleHeadline: In 10 days of Aug, South Goa district hospital sees 71 dengue cases, 27 admissions
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever surged at the South Goa District Hospital in Panaji, Goa. In the first 10 days of August, 71 dengue cases were detected with 27 hospital admissions. Lab detections rose from 9 in May to 39 in June and to 91 in July, with admissions scaling from 8 (May) to 29 (June) to 79 (July) and 27 (August, so far). Medical Superintendent Dr. Rajendra Borkar attributes the spike to pre-monsoon and peri-monsoon conditions, with intermittent rain promoting breeding in clean stagnant water around homes. He notes dengue is an indoor biter and breeder and that there is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive care. The hospital urges people with fever and headache lasting more than 2–3 days to get tested promptly and to implement measures to prevent mosquito breeding in surroundings.

article.articleHeadline: Indian expat in Dubai dies after suspected rat fever during vacation in Kerala
article.articleSummary: An Indian expatriate in Dubai died after a suspected leptospirosis (rat fever) infection contracted during a vacation in Kerala, India. The article, published 2026-08-11, references the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s description of the disease's biphasic illness: initial symptoms include fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, vomiting, and diarrhea; some patients improve briefly before relapse. In severe second phase, kidney or liver failure or meningitis can occur. The report frames this as an imported case from Kerala to Dubai, with no details on laboratory confirmation or broader outbreak status, and no additional case counts mentioned. This highlights potential travel-associated risk of rat fever and the importance of recognizing its two-phase illness in travelers returning from endemic regions.

article.articleHeadline: Seroprevalence of Nipah virus specific antibodies in pigs from regions with reported human cases using recombinant nucleocapsid protein based indirect-ELISA
article.articleSummary: Nipah virus (NiV), a bat-borne zoonosis causing fatal encephalitis in South-East Asia including India, was studied in Kerala pigs using a recombinant nucleocapsid (rN) protein–based indirect-ELISA (NiV-rN-iELISA). The assay showed 84.85% positive and 85.37% negative agreement with the commercial AsurDx™ i-ELISA. Sero-surveillance of 741 pigs across seven Kerala districts during retrospective (2018–2019) and current (2024–2025) periods revealed varying NiV IgG seroprevalence, highest in Ernakulam district at 24.03% and an average of 5.67% across five districts. Hotspot analysis demonstrated significant spatial clustering of seropositivity in specific Kerala taluks, most pronounced in Ernakulam. The NiV-rN-iELISA enables routine serosurveillance at bat–pig–human interfaces to assess spillover risk, refine risk maps, and support strategic control measures.

article.articleHeadline: Chongqing Infectious Disease Expert Liu Min Reminds: Monkeypox Is Nearby; If You Suspect Infection, Where Should You Seek Treatment?
article.articleSummary: Monkeypox is no longer an 'African disease' in China. Mainland China’s first imported case was detected in Chongqing in September 2022, with a local outbreak in August 2024. From 2023–2026 monthly reports show ongoing cases: January 28, March 28, April 32, May 86; most locally acquired belong to lineage IIb; no deaths reported. Transmission is via close skin-to-skin contact and sexual contact, with men who have sex with men and HIV-positive individuals disproportionately affected (over 40%). Incubation is 5–21 days (commonly 6–13). Signs include fever ≥38.5°C, lymphadenopathy, and a vesiculopustular rash beginning on the face/oral region and possibly involving genitals/anal area, lasting 2–4 weeks. Diagnosis relies on PCR from lesion samples; rapid testing is available at Chongqing Public Health Medical Rescue Center. No domestically approved vaccine yet; vaccines exist in Hong Kong, Macau, and Thailand; a Chinese mRNA vaccine entered US/China trials in 2026. Prevention emphasizes avoiding close skin contact and high-risk sexual behavior; most patients recover with supportive care; seek Infectious Diseases Department care promptly.

article.articleHeadline: Practice to Build Defenses, Practice to Prepare for Battle — Guoluo Prefecture and Maduo County Jointly Conduct a Real-World Plague Emergency Response Drill
article.articleSummary: On August 9, 2026, Guoluo Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture and Maduo County in Qinghai Province jointly conducted a real-world plague emergency response drill to bolster plateau public health defenses and cross-regional response capabilities. Led by the prefecture health commission and county authorities, the exercise involved prefecture/county CDCs, health bureaus, emergency management, and over 50 staff, with police, county hospital, and township clinics participating and department heads observing. The drill simulated a live plague outbreak and covered emergency mobilization, personal protective measures, epidemiological investigation, close-contact tracing, specimen collection and transport, site disinfection and flea control, risk assessment, reporting, and cross-regional joint prevention and control, strictly adhering to biosafety standards. Maduo County will summarize lessons, refine contingency plans, and sustain routine, practical drills to strengthen plague surveillance, environmental disinfection, and health education, safeguarding public health.

article.articleHeadline: Be cautious during summer vacation: a bite from this insect may cause a parasitic infection.
article.articleSummary: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is a chronic parasitic disease in China, caused by Leishmania and transmitted by Phlebotomine sandflies (white sand fly). High risk during summer holidays; sandflies are active May–September, peak June–July; major endemic regions include Beijing, Hebei, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Henan, Gansu, Xinjiang, and Sichuan, with scattered cases as transmission persists. Infection occurs when a sandfly bites an infected dog and then bites a person. incubation 3–6 months; symptoms: prolonged irregular fever, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia; often atypical and misdiagnosed. Diagnosis relies on exposure history and lab tests: bone marrow aspiration, rk39 rapid test, or PCR. Treatment with sodium stibogluconate is effective under medical supervision; alternatives include amphotericin B for resistant or special patients. Preventive measures: bed nets, clothing, repellents, and post-travel testing of pets (antibody testing within six months). Emphasize early recognition and treatment to reduce mortality.

article.articleHeadline: Viral Marker Strategies Boost Hepatitis B Cure Prediction
article.articleSummary: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) management advances toward a functional cure, defined as sustained loss of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), with covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) persistence preventing complete eradication. A China-based team led by Prof. Qishui Ou and Prof. Zhen Xun at Fujian Medical University reviewed HBV viral markers for predicting functional cure. Published June 27, 2026 in Portal Hypertension & Cirrhosis, they find quantitative HBsAg (qHBsAg) remains the most clinically valuable single predictor, with baseline levels and early declines during Peg-IFN-α therapy informing sustained HBsAg clearance. Multimarker models incorporating additional viral markers often outperform single markers, though qHBsAg is most cost-effective in primary care settings with limited testing resources. The authors propose a framework for pretreatment stratification, monitoring response, timing NA discontinuation, and consolidating after HBsAg loss, integrating host factors and future AI/high-sensitivity assays to personalize CHB care and advance WHO elimination goals.

article.articleHeadline: Don't take being scratched or licked by cats or dogs lightly — one action to assess infection risk.
article.articleSummary: In Zhejiang, China, a park encounter left a woman with high-risk rabies exposure after a stray dog licked a torn toe; she had paronychia with skin break. Rabies is nearly universally fatal once symptoms appear, and about 95% of global human cases are dog-mediated. Transmission occurs through broken skin or mucous membranes; high-risk animals include stray cats, wolves, foxes, skunks, and bats. The case highlights the 2023 Rabies Exposure Prevention and Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Work Specification. Exposure levels: Level 1—no skin injury; Level 2—scratch or minor bleeding from a high-risk animal; Level 3—severe bite/scratch with bleeding or mucosal contact, requiring wound cleansing, vaccination, and possibly passive immunization. Emphasizes prompt care; even seemingly healthy pets can spread rabies. If persistent red marks or tingling indicate possible skin barrier damage, seek evaluation at a rabies exposure clinic.

article.articleSummary: Shenzhen, China — A 41-year-old man developed Legionella pneumophila pneumonia after using a home air conditioner that had not been cleaned. On July 13 he presented with cough, dyspnea and multi-organ dysfunction; CT showed left-lung consolidation with severe hypoxemia, and he was admitted to the ICU. He received high-flow oxygen and antibacterial therapy, plus aggressive fluid removal (about 11 kg lost in three days). Despite diuresis, respiratory status worsened; July 16 CT showed progression. Lung lavage identified Legionella pneumophila within ~22 hours. The infection stemmed from the air conditioner's cooling-water system; aerosols likely inspired by the AC. He was managed with noninvasive ventilation and careful positioning; antibiotics tailored to Legionella. By July 22 fever and markers declined and CT improved; he was moved from ICU to nephrology on July 23 and discharged August 1. Advice: clean ACs regularly, ensure ventilation, and preserve water system hygiene to prevent Legionella.

article.articleHeadline: How to Keep Flies from Laying Eggs in Food, Prevent the Risk of Disease
article.articleSummary: Houseflies can contaminate food with microbes and potentially lay eggs, raising disease risk. The article notes intestinal myiasis as a possible, though rare, outcome when fly larvae develop in the digestive tract after ingestion of contaminated food. Flies carry bacteria from waste, animal carcasses, or spoiled food, making hygiene crucial. If a fly only lands briefly on food, the contamination risk is lower; longer contact increases microbial transfer. Practical, non-chemical methods to repel or trap flies include: apple cider vinegar traps with sugar and dish soap; using jars of rotting fruit with perforated lids; planting aromas flies dislike (basil, mint, lavender, cloves, cinnamon) or using essential oils, diffusers, or scented candles; and simple candle traps placed over shallow water. Flies do not have teeth and liquefy foods, so surface contamination and microbial transfer are the main concern. Keep food covered to prevent eggs or microbes from reaching food.

article.articleHeadline: Analysis | The recurring risk: as with Zika, Oropouche virus can affect the brains of fetuses during gestation.
article.articleSummary: Oropouche virus has expanded its circulation in Brazil, with nearly 14,000 confirmed cases in 2024 and elevated counts into 2025, now circulating across all five regions. The expansion accompanies reports of vertical transmission, abortions, fetal deaths, and congenital malformations including microcephaly in pregnancies with infection. To study brain impact, researchers used human cerebral organoids—mini-brains—derived from stem cells. Infections used two lineages: BeAn19991 (Amazonas, 1960) and RJ/LVM-2024 (Rio de Janeiro, 2024) with a rearranged genome. Across both, 657 genes were differential expressed: downregulation of neural progenitor proliferation and upregulation of inflammatory, replication, and cell-death pathways. Organoids showed reduced growth, irregular borders, and disorganization, especially in ventricular zones where progenitors proliferate; Ki67 and PAX6 declined. Neurons and astrocytes were later infected. Similar neurotoxic effects across strains suggest inherent neurotropism, not a recent evolution.

article.articleHeadline: Meningococcal meningitis in childhood: understand the disease and the importance of prevention.
article.articleSummary: As of September 2025, Brazil recorded 696 meningococcal meningitis cases and 131 deaths, following 1,551 cases and 333 deaths in 2023–2024 (monthly averages rising from 60 to 68). Neisseria meningitidis serogroups A, B, C, W, and Y circulate in Brazil with regional variation; serogroup B is among the most common. The disease progresses rapidly, often within 12–24 hours, potentially causing meningitis or septicemia, with about 40% of survivors experiencing sequelae such as deafness, amputations, or neurological impairment. Vaccination is the main preventive strategy: meningococcal C protects only serogroup C; ACWY covers A, C, W, Y; B targets serogroup B. Public health programs offer vaccines C and ACWY; private networks also provide B. Additional measures include hand hygiene, covering coughs, ventilation, and avoiding crowding. Early diagnosis and treatment markedly reduce mortality (Brazil’s fatality reached 22% in 2024).

article.articleHeadline: In 2016, Singapore began releasing millions of non-biting male mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia. Years later, the bold experiment produced one of the world's most successful dengue-control
article.articleSummary: Singapore began releasing Wolbachia-infected male Aedes aegypti in 2016 to suppress dengue transmission. The males do not bite; when they mate with females lacking the same Wolbachia strain, their eggs do not hatch, reducing the vector population over time. Singapore now releases more than 10 million mosquitoes per week, the largest public-sector deployment of Wolbachia technology. A New England Journal of Medicine study found the intervention significantly reduced Aedes aegypti density and lowered dengue risk by more than 70%. Wolbachia blocks transmission of dengue, Zika and chikungunya, though mosquitoes can still bite. Globally, programs exist in Colombia (World Mosquito Program began Medellin in 2015, later Cali; dengue cases in Antioquia reportedly fell by 95%), Indonesia and Brazil, with plans in El Salvador. In the United States, another Wolbachia-based approach uses male tiger mosquitoes for residential control. Efficacy is influenced by local geography and intervention scale.

article.articleHeadline: Rio Grande-based startup develops a tuberculosis diagnostic device.
article.articleSummary: Rio Grande, Brazil-based startup Nernst, housed at the Federal University of Rio Grande (FURG) and incubated in Innovatio, is validating a portable tuberculosis diagnostic device designed to deliver results in five minutes, versus about two hours with current bench methods. The system uses a sputum sample and a biosensor strip within a handheld unit that features a display, enabling point-of-care testing in clinics or remote regions. Derived from doctoral work by Ana Paula Lopes, the device aims to cut costs by ~70% and reduce required sample volume by ~98% compared with traditional diagnostics. The seven-person team collaborates with FURG labs and Tecnopuc in Porto Alegre, supported by the Hangar program, with commercialization anticipated around 2029. Looking ahead, the platform could offer multi-disease readouts, including tuberculosis, COVID-19, Chagas disease, and dengue.

The new molecule shows diagnostic efficacy in both humans and dogs using the same antigen, addressing the urban/peri-urban reservoir role of domestic dogs for Leishmania infantum in Brazil and supporting integrated disease surveillance. Visceral leishmaniasis is potentially fatal and targets liver, spleen, and bone marrow; early, reliable diagnostics are central to control.

article.articleHeadline: El Niño Puts 756 Latin American Hospitals at Risk as Dengue Cases Top 624,000
article.articleSummary: 624,085 suspected dengue cases across the Americas through epidemiological week 12 of 2026, with Brazil adding 62,707 suspected cases in the first five weeks of the year—a 64% drop from the same period in 2025, though uptrends may resume. In 2025, 4.46 million suspected and 1.68 million confirmed dengue cases were reported region-wide, including 8,966 severe cases and 2,207 deaths. Brazil bore the largest burden in 2025: 1.66 million probable cases, 1.45 million confirmed, 1,793 deaths; incidence 775.7 per 100,000. All four dengue serotypes circulated in Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Mexico, Panama, and Puerto Rico. A July 2026 PAHO analysis warns El Niño 2026-2027 could expose 756 emergency hospitals to coastal flooding; drought may paradoxically boost transmission via open-water storage. PAHO’s response emphasizes surveillance, vector control, clinical training, and vaccine guidance, while noting climate disruptions could delay campaigns.

article.articleHeadline: Flesh-eating larva has already infected more than 500 people in Mexico.
article.articleSummary: New World screwworm fly–induced myiasis has infected more than 500 people in Mexico. In a study of 202 patients, 72% were men; ages 12–93 (mean 61), with 77% having at least one comorbidity such as diabetes, alcoholism, cancer or skin disease. Lesions most often affected legs and feet (55%), followed by head and neck (including nose and eyes); infections also occurred on arms, trunk, ears and genitals. Without treatment, myiasis can invade muscle, cartilage and bone, causing infection, sepsis and death. Mexico eradicated the fly in 2003; a Panama barrier was breached in 2022. Since 2024 animal cases rose; USDA cites over 36,000 animal cases in Mexico, with nearly 2,000 active as of Aug 5. In the US, first animal cases appeared in Texas in June (45 total); no travel-associated human cases reported. Brazil reports elderly cases, including an 87-year-old woman who died in Ribeirão Preto after oral/nasal larvae.

article.articleHeadline: Hand, foot, and mouth disease on the rise as school resumes: learn how to prevent.
article.articleSummary: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) is rising as children return to schools in São Paulo, Brazil. Coxsackievirus and Enterovirus A71 drive transmission; HFMD is highly contagious and spreads via respiratory secretions, feces, saliva, and contaminated objects. In São Paulo, 724 cases were recorded January–June this year; nationwide, 2024–2025 cases rose from 5,201 to 6,242 (about 20% increase). During the July–August seasonal peak, increases climbed 171% in 2024 and 248% in 2025. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, malaise, loss of appetite, and painful oral lesions with possible rashes on hands and feet; dehydration risk if oral intake is poor. Diagnosis is clinical; there is no antiviral treatment; management is supportive with fever and pain control and hydration. Prevention centers on handwashing, cleaning toys and surfaces, not sharing cups and utensils, and temporarily separating ill children from schools; return only when fever-free and clinically better. Dr. Caroline Peev of Sabará Hospital Infantil notes strong post-vacation transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Be vigilant for RSV-related pneumonia during the rainy season; the elderly are at risk of severe complications - The Bangkok Insight.
article.articleSummary: Thailand’s Department of Disease Control warns RSV-related pneumonia, influenza, and COVID-19 should be monitored during the rainy season. RSV infection is rising; Digital Disease Surveillance (Jan 1–Apr 30, 2569) recorded 1,792 RSV cases (17.358 per 100,000) with no deaths. RSV can affect all ages but may progress to lower respiratory tract disease and pneumonia requiring hospitalization, especially in the elderly and those with diabetes, COPD, or heart disease, or immunocompromised individuals. Pneumonia in 2569 data (Jan 1–Feb 26) reached 63,511 cases with 73 deaths; incidence in people aged 60+ was 237.70 per 100,000. RSV spreads via droplets, secretions, and surfaces that can harbor the virus for hours. Vaccination guidance from the Infectious Diseases Association of Thailand targets adults and seniors: 75+, or 50–74 with comorbidities (lung/heart disease, immunocompromise, diabetes with complications, severe obesity, liver or advanced kidney disease, or kidney transplant). Seek care for fever, cough, or shortness of breath.

article.articleHeadline: Only 8% of people in UK check rabies risk before travelling abroad, despite it existing in over 75% of countries
article.articleSummary: Rabies remains a global travel health threat, present in more than 150 countries and causing about 59,000 deaths annually. UK and Northern Ireland travellers show a striking underestimation of risk: only 8% check whether rabies is present at a destination, and 26.4% verify vaccination requirements. Nearly half (43%) have travelled to rabies-present destinations in the last five years without verifying risk; in Northern Ireland, 52% have done so, while 70% would delay or avoid seeking medical care after exposure and 70% are unaware that rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms develop. Gaps include 62% not knowing cats or other mammals can transmit rabies, 49% unaware transmission via bite, and 61% unaware of lick/scratch transmission. About 99% of human cases arise from dog bites. A 2025 fatal case in Morocco underscores risk. Campaigns Think Rabies Before You Travel and Mission Rabies promote precautions and dog vaccination in hotspots; cited destinations include Turkey, Morocco, and Thailand.

article.articleHeadline: The Silent Resistance: Rethinking Ghana's Battle Against Mosquitoes
article.articleSummary: Ghana's battle against mosquitoes amid rising malaria cases is confronted by insecticide resistance and reliance on adult sprays. As of August 10, 2026, communities widely use synthetic chemical sprays and bed nets, yet vectors adapt gradually, eroding effectiveness and signaling control failures through increasing disease burden. Rapid urbanization, poor drainage, expanding irrigation, and climate shifts expand breeding sites, intensifying the challenge. The article promotes Bacillus thuringiensis var. israelensis (Bti) as a proven, accessible larvicidal option that targets larvae in stagnant water, offering minimal cost and time and zero harm to aquatic life. Emphasizing early-stage biological larviciding reframes vector management from reactive chemical dependence to proactive source-control. Normalizing larviciding at local breeding sites—before adult mosquitoes emerge—could reduce vector populations and better protect communities from mosquito-borne diseases.

article.articleHeadline: Impact of Climate Change on Africa's Malaria Map.
article.articleSummary: Nature’s late-July study shows climate change reshapes Africa’s malaria map. While anomalous warming generally boosts malaria, effects vary by region. Rising temperatures are projected to increase malaria risk in southern Africa and East Africa’s highlands, but may reduce transmission in current hotspots that become too hot for mosquitoes. In major West African countries—Nigeria, Burkina Faso, and Mali—cases could decline by about 5%. In very hot Sahel nations Niger, the Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Somalia, malaria could disappear as conditions become inhospitable for vectors. Cooler, historically non-endemic areas such as the southern parts of Africa and East Africa’s highlands face higher risk, with around 5% increases reported in the Ethiopian Highlands, Kenya, Burundi, and similar rises in Angola, Zambia, and northeastern South Africa. By 2100, malaria risk could reach 20% in the Rift Valley and southern coastal Africa. Limiting warming to 2C could avert roughly five cases per 1,000 children in southern Africa; adaptation and sustained health funding remain essential.
